paragraphs.heading: What wave optics covers
paragraphs.text: Wave optics, also called physical optics, is the part of optics that deals with interference, diffraction, polarization and related effects. These are the cases where the ray picture used in geometric optics stops working. Some effects are usually left out of it, such as quantum noise in optical communication. That topic belongs to a separate sub-branch called coherence theory.

paragraphs.heading: An approximation with the same name
paragraphs.text: The phrase physical optics also names a working approximation used in optics, electrical engineering and applied physics. It sits between two other approaches. Geometric optics ignores wave effects altogether, while full wave electromagnetism is the precise theory. The word "physical" only means the method is more physical than ray optics; it does not mean the method is an exact theory.

paragraphs.heading: How the approximation works
paragraphs.text: The method has two steps. First, ray optics gives an estimate of the field arriving at a surface. Then that field is added up, or integrated, across the whole surface to find the field that is transmitted or scattered. In optics the surface is usually a lens, a mirror or an aperture, which is an opening that light passes through. This is a standard way of estimating diffraction effects.

paragraphs.heading: What it captures and misses
paragraphs.text: The approximation reproduces several interference, diffraction and polarization effects. What it does not capture is the way diffraction depends on polarization. It is a high-frequency approximation, and it is often more accurate for light than for radio. In radio it is still used to estimate some effects that resemble optical ones.

paragraphs.heading: Radar and the lit side
paragraphs.text: In radar scattering, the method looks at the front of an object, the part that the incoming wave lights up directly. At each point there, it borrows the current that would be found on a flat tangent plane made of similar material. Current on the shadowed parts is set to zero. The scattered field is then found by integrating over these estimated currents. This works well for large, smooth, convex bodies and for lossy surfaces, which reflect little.

paragraphs.heading: Weak spots and a fix
paragraphs.text: The ray-based estimate is generally poor near edges and near the boundaries of shadows. It can be improved there by adding calculations for diffraction and for creeping waves. The standard theory also has defects for scattered fields, and its accuracy drops away from the specular direction. An improved theory introduced in 2004 gives exact solutions for wave diffraction by conducting scatterers.
